warmup.q: fun entries(): Flow<LedgerEntry> = flow { println("fetching"); emit(api.firstPage()) }. You call val f = entries() and then f.collect { } twice. How many times does fetching print?
options: Once, at the first collect; the second one reuses the values
Twice: the body runs again for every collector
Never: println inside a flow builder is ignored
warmup.why: A flow { } is cold. Calling entries() only builds a description of the work, and the body runs from the top each time someone collects it. Nothing is cached between collectors, which is also why a retry can simply collect again.

sections.h: A flow is a recipe that runs once per collector
sections.html:
A Flow<T> is a stream of values that you receive one at a time through a suspend call. The usual way to make one is the flow { } builder, where you call emit once per value:

Java
// Java equivalent: a cold Flux that asks for the next page once the previous one is in
Flux<LedgerEntry> ledgerEntries(LedgerApi api, String accountId) {
    return api.page(accountId, null)                                      // Mono<LedgerPage>
        .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : api.page(accountId, p.nextCursor()))
        .flatMapIterable(LedgerPage::entries);
}
Kotlin
fun ledgerEntries(api: LedgerApi, accountId: String): Flow<LedgerEntry> = flow {
    var cursor: String? = null
    do {
        val page = api.page(accountId, cursor)   // a suspend call to the ledger service
        page.entries.forEach { emit(it) }
        cursor = page.nextCursor
    } while (cursor != null)
}

Calling ledgerEntries(...) runs nothing. It returns a description of the work, like a recipe. The body runs when someone calls a terminal operator such as collect, and it runs again from the top for every collector. That is a cold flow. A Reactor Flux is cold in the same way (lesson 2 of the reactive track): nothing happens until you subscribe.

Two properties follow from the design. A flow is sequential: emit is a suspend call that returns only when the collector has finished with the value, so the producer never runs ahead of the consumer. That is Flow's backpressure, and there is no request(n) in sight. And a collector that stops early stops the producer. take(3) cancels the flow after the third value, so the flow { } body never asks for a page it doesn't need.

The other builders are shortcuts. flowOf(a, b, c) emits fixed values, and list.asFlow() or (1..n).asFlow() turn collections and ranges into flows. Remember from lesson 5 of this track that asFlow() doesn't check for cancellation between items, so add .cancellable() when a long one has to stop on time. channelFlow and callbackFlow are for producers that aren't plain sequential code, and lesson 9 of this track covers them.

A flow returned from a function is almost always cold. The exceptions are the hot flows, StateFlow and SharedFlow, which keep running whether or not anyone collects. They are lesson 8 of this track.

alt.html: // Java equivalent of ColdFlow.kt: a Reactor Flux is cold too. Nothing runs until you subscribe, // every subscription starts again, and take(3) cancels the source when it has enough. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ColdFlowJava { static Flux<String> entries(String accountId) { return Flux.range(0, 3) .concatMap(page -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> { System.out.println(" fetching page " + page + " of " + accountId); return List.of("e" + (page * 2 + 1), "e" + (page * 2 + 2)); }).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(20)), 1) // prefetch 1: ask for one page at a time .flatMapIterable(entries -> entries); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("building the flux"); Flux<String> flux = entries("acc-1"); System.out.println("built; nothing fetched yet"); System.out.println("first subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + flux.collectList().block()); System.out.println("second subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + flux.collectList().block()); System.out.println("take(3):"); System.out.println(" got " + flux.take(3).collectList().block()); } }

try.expect: Building prints nothing. Each full collection fetches pages 0, 1 and 2 again. take(3) fetches pages 0 and 1, because the third entry is on page 1, and the flow is cancelled before page 2. With take(2) only page 0 is fetched. The Java twin prints the same lines, because a Flux is cold too.

sections.h: Intermediate operators build the pipeline, terminal operators run it
sections.html:
Operators come in two kinds. Intermediate operators such as map, filter, onEach, take and transform take a flow and return a new flow. They are plain functions, they return at once, and they run nothing. Terminal operators such as collect, toList, first, single, fold and count are suspend functions. They start the flow, consume it, and return when it ends.

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor operators also only build; block() (or subscribe) runs them
Flux<String> receipts = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1")
    .filter(e -> e.amountCents() > 0)
    .map(e -> String.format("EUR %.2f", e.amountCents() / 100.0));
List<String> firstTen = receipts.take(10).collectList().block();
Kotlin
val receipts: Flow<String> = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1")    // nothing runs yet
    .filter { it.amountCents > 0 }
    .map { "EUR %.2f".format(it.amountCents / 100.0) }
val firstTen = receipts.take(10).toList()                   // now it runs

By default all of it runs in one coroutine, one value at a time. The first entry travels through filter, through map and into the collector before the flow body produces the second. There are no queues between the stages and no extra threads. The few operators that add concurrency on purpose, such as buffer, flowOn and flatMapMerge, say so in their docs.

A reusable operator is just an extension function, and it reads like a built-in:

Java
// Java equivalent: a function from Flux to Flux, applied with transform
static Flux<LedgerEntry> settledOnly(Flux<LedgerEntry> entries) {
    return entries.filter(e -> e.status() == Status.SETTLED);
}

Flux<LedgerEntry> settled = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1").transform(Ledger::settledOnly);
Kotlin
fun Flow<LedgerEntry>.settledOnly(): Flow<LedgerEntry> = filter { it.status == Status.SETTLED }

val settled = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1").settledOnly()

transform { value -> ... } is the general form: it can emit zero, one or many values for each input.

Watch for a terminal operator hiding in a function that ought to return a flow. suspend fun receipts(): List<String> = pipeline.toList() runs the whole export at the call and holds every line in memory. fun receipts(): Flow<String> leaves the caller free to stream, take the first ten, or stop on an error.

Then each amount goes all the way through before the next one is emitted: emit 4250, filter passed, map, collect, then emit -990, which stops at the filter, then the third amount. With take(1) only one emit prints: once the collector has its value, the flow is cancelled. The synchronous Flux in the Java twin prints the same order.

sections.h: Move the upstream with flowOn, not with withContext around emit
sections.html:
A flow runs in the context of the coroutine that collects it. The docs call this context preservation, and it means the code that collects never has to wonder which thread its lambda runs on. It also rules out the obvious way to move a blocking source, such as the acquirer's settlement file read through a legacy blocking reader, to IO:

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor has no such rule; subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler
Flux.<SettlementRecord>generate(sink -> {
        String line = reader.readLine();
        if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parse(line));
    })
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
Kotlin
// wrong: emit from another context throws IllegalStateException ("Flow invariant is violated")
flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(parse(reader.readLine()!!)) } }

// right: flowOn changes the context of everything above it
flow {
    while (true) emit(parse(reader.readLine() ?: break))
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)

emit must run in the collector's context, and the builder checks every call. flowOn(ctx) is the tool. It changes the context of the flow above it, the upstream, and leaves everything below it, the collector included, where it was. You can use it more than once, and each one covers the operators up to the previous flowOn.

To do that, flowOn has to run the upstream in a separate coroutine, so when the dispatcher changes it puts a channel between the two halves. The KDoc says it buffers "similarly to buffer operator", with the default buffer size. The upstream can therefore run ahead of the collector by up to 64 values instead of exactly one. For a file read that is usually what you want.

Reactor's nearest tools are subscribeOn, which moves the source, and publishOn, which moves what follows it (lesson 6 of the reactive track). The difference that matters is the subscriber. With Reactor, unless you add a publishOn, your subscriber runs on the scheduler's thread too. With flowOn, the collector always stays in its own context.

So don't reach for flowOn to move the collector. If the collecting side blocks (it writes each line to a file, say), wrap the terminal call instead: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { flow.collect { writer.write(it) } }.

code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext private fun thread() = Thread.currentThread().name fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { if (args.firstOrNull() == "wrong") { try { flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit("pay-1,4250,EUR") } // emit from another context }.collect { println("collected $it") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("IllegalStateException: " + e.message!!.lines().first()) } return@runBlocking } flow { for (line in listOf("pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,-990,EUR")) { Thread.sleep(50) // a blocking file read println("read on ${thread()}") emit(line) } } .map { println("parse on ${thread()}"); parse(it) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // everything above this line runs on IO .map { println("format on ${thread()}"); "${it.first}: ${it.second} cents" } .collect { println("save on ${thread()} $it") } } private fun parse(line: String): Pair<String, Long> = line.split(",").let { it[0] to it[1].toLong() }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowOnDemo.kt: Reactor's subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler, // and publishOn moves everything after it. Without a publishOn, the subscriber runs on that // scheduler's thread too, which is the difference from flowOn. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class FlowOnDemoJava { static String thread() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.fromIterable(List.of("pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,-990,EUR")) .doOnNext(line -> { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // a blocking file read System.out.println("read on " + thread()); }) .map(line -> { System.out.println("parse on " + thread()); return line.split(","); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // the source and the steps above run there .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) // the steps below move to another thread .map(f -> { System.out.println("format on " + thread()); return f[0] + ": " + f[1] + " cents"; }) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println("save on " + thread() + " " + s)) .blockLast(); } }

try.expect: read and parse run on a DefaultDispatcher-worker thread, while format and save run on main. After the move, format joins them on the worker, but save stays on main: no flowOn can move the collector. With -Pargs=wrong you get IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated. The Java twin needs subscribeOn for the source and publishOn to move the later steps to single-1.

sections.h: Handle upstream errors with catch, and every ending with onCompletion
sections.html:
Flows promise exception transparency. An exception thrown downstream, by an operator below or by the collector, belongs to the downstream, and a flow must not catch it and carry on emitting. The error-handling operators are built around that rule.

catch { e -> ... } handles exceptions from the flow above it. It can log, emit a fallback, or rethrow. Exceptions thrown below it, including inside collect { }, pass straight through to whoever called collect.

Java
// Java equivalent: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it; doFinally runs on every exit
settlementRecords(file)
    .<ImportEvent>map(r -> new Imported(r.paymentId()))
    .doFinally(signal -> metrics.importEnded(signal))
    .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage())))
    .doOnNext(ledger::save)
    .blockLast();
Kotlin
settlementRecords(file)                                         // may throw IOException
    .map<SettlementRecord, ImportEvent> { ImportEvent.Imported(it.paymentId) }
    .onCompletion { cause -> metrics.importEnded(cause) }      // sees every way the flow ends
    .catch { e -> emit(ImportEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) }   // upstream failures only
    .collect { ledger.save(it) }                                // a failure here reaches the caller

onCompletion { cause -> } is the flow's finally. It runs once, however the flow ends. cause is null after a normal end, the exception after a failure upstream or downstream, and a CancellationException when the collector stopped early, as take and first do. Unlike catch, it handles nothing: the exception carries on after it. Put it above catch to see the original error, or below to see only what got past.

The classic way to break the rule is a try/catch around emit inside a builder. emit runs the downstream code, so that catch also catches the collector's exceptions. If it then emits again, the flow throws IllegalStateException ("Flow exception transparency is violated"). That is one of the bugs in this lesson's lab. Use catch instead, which knows where it sits.

One more benefit of cold flows shows up here. retry(3) and retryWhen { cause, attempt -> ... } recover by collecting the upstream again, and that works only because the recipe can be run again from the top.

Flow's error model is close to Reactor's. In both, a step that can fail goes above the error operator if you want it handled (onEach above catch, doOnNext above onErrorResume), and anything below it is the subscriber's problem. One difference makes Flow simpler: a failure in the collector is an ordinary exception thrown out of collect, so a plain try around the terminal call catches it.

code.title: CatchDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onCompletion import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val failIn = args.firstOrNull() ?: "upstream" // or "collector" val lines = flow { emit("pay-1,4250,EUR") emit("pay-2,-990,EUR") if (failIn == "upstream") throw IOException("settlement file truncated") emit("pay-3,120000,GBP") } try { lines .map { it.substringBefore(",") } .onCompletion { cause -> println("onCompletion: cause = $cause") } .catch { e -> println("catch: $e"); emit("ABORTED") } .collect { id -> println("collect $id") if (failIn == "collector" && id == "pay-2") throw IllegalStateException("ledger db down") } println("collect returned normally") } catch (e: Exception) { println("the caller got: $e") } }

alt.title: CatchDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of CatchDemo.kt: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it, like catch, // and doFinally runs on every way out, like onCompletion. An exception thrown in the subscriber's // own lambda is not an upstream error: no operator above it gets to "handle" it. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class CatchDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String failIn = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "upstream"; // or "collector" Flux<String> lines = Flux.concat( Flux.just("pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,-990,EUR"), failIn.equals("upstream") ? Flux.error(new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("settlement file truncated"))) : Flux.just("pay-3,120000,GBP")); try { lines .map(l -> l.substring(0, l.indexOf(','))) .doFinally(signal -> System.out.println("doFinally: signal = " + signal)) .onErrorResume(e -> { System.out.println("onErrorResume: " + e); return Flux.just("ABORTED"); }) .doOnNext(id -> { System.out.println("consume " + id); if (failIn.equals("collector") && id.equals("pay-2")) throw new IllegalStateException("ledger db down"); }) .blockLast(); System.out.println("blockLast returned normally"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("the caller got: " + e); } } }

try.expect: Upstream failure: pay-1 and pay-2 are collected, onCompletion prints the IOException, catch prints it and emits ABORTED, which is collected, and collect returns normally. Collector failure: onCompletion prints the IllegalStateException, catch prints nothing, and the caller gets ledger db down. The Java twin matches: onErrorResume only handles the upstream error, and doFinally reports onError or cancel.

analogy: A cold flow is a recipe card, not a pot of soup. Writing the card (calling flow { } and chaining map and filter) cooks nothing. Each diner who orders (each collect) gets the recipe cooked from scratch, one plate at a time, and the cook doesn't start the next plate until the diner has taken the last one. A diner who says "that's enough" (take) stops the cooking. flowOn moves the cooking to another kitchen while the diner stays at the same table. catch is the cook's rule for kitchen accidents, such as serving a fallback dish when the oven breaks, and it has nothing to say about a diner who drops their plate. The analogy breaks on cost: a real kitchen would never cook the same meal twice for two diners, and a flow does exactly that unless you share it, which is lesson 8 of this track.
world: Flows fit the streaming jobs in a payments platform. A statement export can stream ledger pages straight to the file instead of loading two million rows into a list. A settlement-file import can read the acquirer's file with a blocking reader under flowOn(Dispatchers.IO), map each line to a ledger posting, report progress in onCompletion, and turn a truncated file into one Aborted event with catch. Two habits keep them honest. Put work that can fail and must be covered by catch (such as saving each record) in onEach above the catch, then call collect() with no lambda. And keep blocking JDBC or file reads above a flowOn, never inside withContext around emit. For a JDBC cursor, opening and closing the connection inside the flow { } body means each collector gets its own connection, and onCompletion or finally releases it however the flow ends.
mistake: The most common mistake is treating .catch { } at the end of a chain as a try/catch around the whole pipeline, including the collect { } lambda. It isn't: catch handles only the flow above it, so an exception thrown while saving a record in collect sails past it and fails the caller. People expect otherwise because every other error handler they know wraps everything inside it. The fix is to move the work that can fail upstream of catch, the pattern the Kotlin docs show: records.onEach { ledger.save(it) }.catch { e -> log.warn("import failed", e) }.collect(). If the caller should see the failure instead, drop the catch and let it propagate.

compare.title: A settlement import: Flux vs Flow

java.title: SettlementImport.java
java.html: Flux<ImportEvent> importFile(LineReader reader) { return Flux.<SettlementRecord>generate(sink -> { // 1. a cold source, pulled on demand String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parse(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .<ImportEvent>map(r -> new Imported(r.paymentId())) .doFinally(signal -> metrics.importEnded(signal)) // 3. every ending .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage()))); // 4. upstream errors only }

kotlin.title: SettlementImport.kt
kotlin.html: fun importFile(reader: LineReader): Flow<ImportEvent> = flow { // 1. a cold source, plain sequential code while (true) emit(parse(reader.readLine() ?: break)) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .map<SettlementRecord, ImportEvent> { ImportEvent.Imported(it.paymentId) } .onCompletion { cause -> metrics.importEnded(cause) } // 3. every ending .catch { e -> emit(ImportEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) } // 4. upstream errors only

compare.note: The shapes line up step for step, and both are cold. The source is where they differ most. Reactor needs a generator callback with an explicit sink, because a Flux source must answer request(n) from subscribers. A Flow source is an ordinary loop: emit suspends until the collector is ready, so backpressure comes from suspension. Threads differ too. subscribeOn moves the whole chain until a publishOn moves it again, so Reactor subscribers often end up on a scheduler thread. flowOn moves only the upstream, and the collector stays in its own coroutine context. The error operators are nearly identical: catch and onErrorResume both handle only what is above them, and onCompletion and doFinally both run on every ending.

worked.title: Stream a statement export instead of loading it

steps.say: A statement export loads every ledger entry for the month into a list, formats it, and writes the file. For a merchant with two million entries the pod runs out of heap, and nothing is written until all the pages are in.
steps.code: suspend fun exportStatement(accountId: String, out: Path) { val all = mutableListOf<LedgerEntry>() var cursor: String? = null do { val page = api.page(accountId, cursor) all += page.entries // every entry held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Files.write(out, all.filter { it.amountCents != 0L }.map(::format)) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same design: collect everything, then write void exportStatement(String accountId, Path out) throws IOException { List<LedgerEntry> all = new ArrayList<>(); String cursor = null; do { LedgerPage page = api.page(accountId, cursor); all.addAll(page.entries()); // every entry held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor(); } while (cursor != null); Files.write(out, all.stream().filter(e -> e.amountCents() != 0).map(Export::format).toList()); }

steps.say: Make the source a cold flow. Only one page is in memory at a time, and the next page is fetched only when the writer has caught up.
steps.code: // 1. the source: pages on demand fun ledgerEntries(accountId: String): Flow<LedgerEntry> = flow { var cursor: String? = null do { val page = api.page(accountId, cursor) page.entries.forEach { emit(it) } cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) }

alt.html: // 1. the source: pages on demand Flux<LedgerEntry> ledgerEntries(String accountId) { return api.page(accountId, null) .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : api.page(accountId, p.nextCursor())) .flatMapIterable(LedgerPage::entries); }

steps.say: Build the pipeline with intermediate operators, and write in the collector. The file write blocks, and it is on the collecting side, so it moves with withContext around the terminal call. flowOn wouldn't help: it never moves the collector.
steps.code: suspend fun exportStatement(accountId: String, out: Path) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { // 3. the collector's blocking writes run on IO Files.newBufferedWriter(out).use { writer -> ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter { it.amountCents != 0L } // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(::format) .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() } // runs it, one line at a time } }

alt.html: void exportStatement(String accountId, Path out) throws IOException { try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(out)) { ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter(e -> e.amountCents() != 0) // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 3. the blocking writes run elsewhere .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .blockLast(); // runs it } }

steps.say: A half-written statement must not look finished. Delete it when the flow ends with an error. onCompletion sees the cause, and the exception still reaches the caller afterwards, which is what an export job should do.
steps.code: ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter { it.amountCents != 0L } .map(::format) .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause != null) Files.deleteIfExists(out) } // 4. no partial files .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() }

alt.html: ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter(e -> e.amountCents() != 0) .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .doOnError(e -> deleteQuietly(out)) // 4. no partial files .blockLast();

steps.say: Self-check: a caller runs exportStatement(...) inside withTimeout(30.seconds) and the timeout fires halfway. Is the partial file deleted? (Yes. The timeout cancels the coroutine, so the flow ends with a CancellationException, cause is not null, and onCompletion deletes the file. It runs inside the pipeline, before use has closed the writer. Linux doesn't mind, but Windows refuses to delete an open file, so a finally around use is the more portable place for the delete.)

lab.title: A ledger flow, a settlement reader and an importer
steps: Run the tests. Seven of eight fail. LedgerModel.kt holds the API, the reader and the event types.
Write ledgerEntries with flow { }: ask for pages starting with cursor null, emit every entry, and stop when nextCursor is null. The three ledger tests check that it is lazy, cold and stops early.
Fix settlementRecords: delete the withContext and add .flowOn(io) after the builder.
Rewrite importReport as a chain: map each record to Imported, then onCompletion { onDone(it) }, then catch that emits Aborted(message).
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: For ledgerEntries, a do { ... } while (cursor != null) loop inside flow { } is all you need. emit suspends until the collector is done, so take(3) cancels the loop before the next api.page call.
map needs to know it produces the sealed type, not Imported, or catch can't emit Aborted into it. Write .map<SettlementRecord, ImportEvent> { ... }.
Put onCompletion above catch: there it sees the upstream exception itself. Below catch it would see null, because catch turned the failure into a normal end.
No try anywhere in importReport. A try around emit also catches the collector's exceptions, and that breaks exception transparency.

drill.title: A blocking file as a flow, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun chargebacks(reader: LineReader): Flow<Chargeback> that reads lines with the blocking reader.readLine() (null at the end) on Dispatchers.IO, parses each with parseChargeback(line), skips lines whose amount is 0, and emits Chargeback.INVALID_FILE once if reading or parsing fails.

answer.html: fun chargebacks(reader: LineReader): Flow<Chargeback> = flow { while (true) { val line = reader.readLine() ?: break emit(parseChargeback(line)) } } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // the blocking reads, and nothing below .filter { it.amountCents != 0L } .catch { emit(Chargeback.INVALID_FILE) } // upstream failures only

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor Flux<Chargeback> chargebacks(LineReader reader) { return Flux.<Chargeback>generate(sink -> { String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parseChargeback(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // the blocking reads .filter(c -> c.amountCents() != 0) .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(Chargeback.INVALID_FILE)); // upstream failures only }

recap: A Flow is cold: building it runs nothing, and the flow { } body runs from the top for every collector.
Flows are sequential. emit suspends until the collector is done with the value, which gives backpressure for free, and take stops the producer early.
Intermediate operators (map, filter, onEach, take) build a new flow; terminal operators (collect, toList, first) are suspend functions that run it.
A flow runs in its collector's context. Move the upstream with flowOn(dispatcher); emit inside withContext throws "Flow invariant is violated".
catch handles only exceptions from above it, and the collector's exceptions pass through. Never wrap emit in a try.
onCompletion { cause -> } runs on every ending: null for normal, the error for a failure, a CancellationException for an early stop.

explain.prompt: A teammate's import pipeline ends in .catch { log.warn("import failed", it) }.collect { repo.save(it) }. When the database went down, the import failed with an exception instead of logging it, and they think catch is broken. Explain what is going on and how to change the code.
explain.answer: catch only handles exceptions from the part of the chain above it. The save runs in the collect lambda, which is below catch, so when the database failed, the exception went straight to whoever called collect. That's deliberate: flows promise exception transparency, meaning a flow never hides the downstream code's failures. If we want the database failure to be logged the same way, the save has to move above the catch, into onEach, and then we call collect with no lambda: records.onEach { repo.save(it) }.catch { log.warn("import failed", it) }.collect(). If the job should fail on a database outage instead, which is probably better for an import, we leave catch for upstream file errors only and let the save failure propagate.

deeper.html:
Why does a flow check emit so strictly? Because operators rely on it. Every operator in the chain runs in one coroutine and assumes that nothing else calls its downstream at the same time. If emit could be called from another coroutine or thread, map and filter would need locks. The checks for context and for exception transparency are what let ordinary sequential code be a correct stream operator.

When you need to emit from several coroutines, use channelFlow { }. Its send is safe from any coroutine started inside the builder, because a channel sits between the producers and the collector. callbackFlow { } is the same thing for callback APIs, and it requires awaitClose { unregister() } at the end, or it throws when the block returns. Lesson 9 of this track uses both.

The Flow interface itself is "not stable for inheritance", in the words of its KDoc: write flows with the builders, or extend AbstractFlow if you really need a class. That matters if you are tempted to implement Flow on a repository class.

Two older guide examples are worth knowing, because the current Kotlin docs dropped them. A busy flow built with asFlow() doesn't check for cancellation between items, which lesson 5 of this track showed. And buffer(), conflate() and collectLatest change the sequential model on purpose. With a producer that takes 100 ms per item and a collector that takes 300 ms, three items take about (100 + 300) x 3 = 1,200 ms plain, about 100 + 300 x 3 = 1,000 ms with buffer(), and about 700 to 800 ms with conflate(), which skips the middle item. Lesson 9 of this track runs those numbers.
